paras: The threatened lynching of Daniel McDonald took place at Ludington, Michigan, in early June 1881, when a crowd met him at the steamboat landing as officers brought him in on a charge of murdering a boy at a sawmill. The crowd called for him to be lynched, but no organized attempt was made and the sheriffs jailed him.

McDonald had been discharged from Cartier & Filer's mill at Ludington; the Lake County Star said he had whipped a horse and quarreled with the foreman. According to a Ludington dispatch to the Chicago Tribune, James Corbin, a boy of 15, caught him cutting belts at the mill in revenge, and McDonald attacked him so that he soon died. The Star dated the attack to nine o'clock on the evening of May 31 and said the boy named McDonald before dying about 3 o'clock the next morning, while the wire briefs placed the killing on the night of June 1.

McDonald fled to Manistee, where he was arrested (in a saloon, according to a Detroit roundup), and Sheriff Baumann brought him back to Ludington by steamer. A Ludington dispatch dated June 3 said that "a mob of five or six hundred" met him at the dock "last evening" and "made some demonstrations towards lynching." The Star, which placed his arrival on the evening of June 1, wrote that the crowd cried "Lynch him!" and "Hang him!" and that it understood revolver shots were fired on both sides and stones thrown. Both accounts said there was no organized effort to take him, and Sheriffs Moulton and Baumann lodged him in jail.
As of June 3 no examination had been held, and no report of an examination, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The Chicago Tribune printed the killing under the headline "A MURDEROUS RUFFIAN" and gave the crowd a single sentence the next day. Briefs on the killing or the arrest ran in Washington, Memphis, St. Paul and rural Minnesota without mention of the crowd, one of them reporting that the accused had escaped. The Lake County Star gave the fullest account a week later, calling the killing a "dastardly crime" and judging the crowd's demonstration "intended more as a scare for the man than for anything else." The German-language Der Nordstern of St. Cloud opened its brief by calling McDonald a murderer who deserved to be lynched. No paper stated the race of McDonald, of the boy or of the crowd.

The date of the confrontation differs: the Tribune's dispatch implies the evening of June 2, while the Star places it on the evening of June 1, the day of the arrest. The boy's surname also appears as Corwin and Corvin.

bases: A crowd met a prisoner accused of murder at the Ludington wharf with cries to lynch and hang him, but officers jailed him (A3, A7); no report names the race of anyone involved.
A crowd of five or six hundred threatened McDonald over the alleged murder of a boy, but no organized attempt was made and he was jailed alive (A3, A7); this was a threatened lynching, not a killing.

The Chicago Tribune's Ludington dispatch and the Lake County Star's separately written account agree that a large crowd met McDonald at the landing with lynching threats and that officers jailed him (A3, A7).

accounts.label: Ludington dispatch to the Chicago Tribune
accounts.gist: A mob of five or six hundred met McDonald at the dock and made 'some demonstrations towards lynching', but no organized attempt was made and officers jailed him.

accounts.label: Lake County Star (regional weekly)
accounts.gist: A large crowd at the wharf cried 'Lynch him!' and 'Hang him!'; the paper understood shots were fired on both sides and stones thrown, but judged the demonstration mainly a scare; the sheriffs jailed him.

framing.detail: The Tribune reported the crowd in one sentence after headlining the killing 'A MURDEROUS RUFFIAN' and calling it a 'gold-blooded murder'.
The Lake County Star called the killing a 'dastardly crime' and minimized the crowd's threats as 'a scare for the man'.
Der Nordstern opened its brief by calling McDonald a murderer who deserved to be lynched.
